items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Energy stored in a stretched or squashed object"?
items.answer: elastic potential energy
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of elastic potential energy.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a battery-powered torch is described as transferring energy electrically.
items.answer: The current transfers energy from the chemical store of the battery to the lamp, where it is transferred by light and heating to the surroundings.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The current transfers energy from the chemical store of the battery to the lamp, where it is transferred by light and heating to the surroundings. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Energy gets used up." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Energy is never destroyed; it is transferred to other stores, often spreading out as thermal energy in the surroundings.
items.markingKey: Energy is never destroyed; it is transferred to other stores, often spreading out as thermal energy in the surroundings. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Priya released a trolley from different heights on a ramp and measured its speed at the bottom with a light gate.

Release height / m | Speed at bottom / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 1.23 | 1.17 | 1.20
0.2 | 1.75 | 1.75 | 1.75
0.3 | 2.00 | 2.09 | 2.14
0.4 | 2.42 | 2.41 | 2.30
0.5 | 2.64 | 2.60 | 2.60

Calculate the mean speed at bottom when the release height was 0.1 m.
items.markingKey: M1 (1.23 + 1.17 + 1.20) ÷ 3; A1 1.20 m/s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 40 kg object moving at 10 m/s (KE = ½mv²).

Mohammed predicts the outcome of an investigation into how the drop height of a ball affects its bounce height.
(a) Formulate a hypothesis that includes a scientific explanation. [2]
(b) Identify the independent and dependent variables. [2]
(c) State two variables that must be controlled. [1]
(d) Sketch the shape of the graph you would expect if the hypothesis is correct and explain how it would support the hypothesis. [1]
items.answer: (a) If the drop height increases, then the bounce height will increase in proportion, because more GPE is converted to KE and then back to GPE, with a similar fraction lost each time. (b) IV: drop height (50, 100, 150, 200 cm); DV: bounce height measured against a metre rule (or from a video). (c) measuring from the bottom of the ball; surface (the same floor). (d) A graph of the DV against the IV showing the predicted trend; if the data follow this trend within the spread of repeats, the hypothesis is supported.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 testable prediction; 1 scientific reasoning: If the drop height increases, then the bounce height will increase in proportion, because more GPE is converted to KE and then back to GPE, with a similar fraction lost each time. (b) 1 IV: drop height (50, 100, 150, 200 cm); 1 DV: bounce height measured against a metre rule (or from a video). (c) 1 any two of the same ball (balls differ in elasticity); surface (the same floor) (soft surfaces absorb energy); dropped, not thrown (throwing adds kinetic energy); measuring from the bottom of the ball (consistent reference point). (d) 1 graph shape consistent with the hypothesis, linked to support.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the drop height of a ball affects its bounce height. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Fix a metre rule vertically; drop the ball from each height; film the bounce and use slow-motion playback to read the bounce height; repeat five times; calculate means and the ratio bounce ÷ drop height.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (keep the area clear; do not stand on chairs – use a stable step). Model: Fix a metre rule vertically; drop the ball from each height; film the bounce and use slow-motion playback to read the bounce height; repeat five times; calculate means and the ratio bounce ÷ drop height.

items.stem: Describe the energy stores and transfers for a pendulum swinging, and explain why it eventually stops.
items.answer: At the highest point maximum GPE, zero KE; as it swings down GPE → KE (by gravity/forces), maximum KE at the bottom; then KE → GPE as it rises. Each swing some energy is transferred by friction at the pivot and air resistance to the thermal store of the surroundings, so the amplitude decreases until it stops. Total energy is conserved.
items.markingKey: At the highest point maximum GPE, zero KE; as it swings down GPE → KE (by gravity/forces), maximum KE at the bottom; then KE → GPE as it rises. Each swing some energy is transferred by friction at the pivot and air resistance to the thermal store of the surroundings, so the amplitude decreases until it stops. Total energy is conserved.

items.stem: What is the unit of energy?
items.answer: Joule (J)

items.stem: Explain why a moving car has more kinetic energy at higher speed.
items.answer: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples the kinetic energy store.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples the kinetic energy store. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy.
items.answer: Kinetic energy is stored by moving objects and depends on mass and speed; GPE is stored due to height in a gravitational field and depends on mass, g and height.
items.markingKey: Kinetic energy is stored by moving objects and depends on mass and speed; GPE is stored due to height in a gravitational field and depends on mass, g and height. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Amara released a trolley from different heights on a ramp and measured its speed at the bottom with a light gate.

Release height / m | Speed at bottom / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 1.15 | 1.10 | 1.10
0.2 | 1.56 | 1.56 | 1.62
0.3 | 2.03 | 2.02 | 1.97
0.4 | 2.20 | 2.17 | 2.24
0.5 | 2.60 | 2.56 | 2.49

Calculate the mean speed at bottom when the release height was 0.1 m.
items.markingKey: M1 (1.15 + 1.10 + 1.10) ÷ 3; A1 1.12 m/s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Mateo plans to investigate how the drop height of a ball affects its bounce height. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: the same ball; surface (the same floor); dropped, not thrown; measuring from the bottom of the ball
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: the same ball – balls differ in elasticity; surface (the same floor) – soft surfaces absorb energy; dropped, not thrown – throwing adds kinetic energy; measuring from the bottom of the ball – consistent reference point. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Gravity-powered lamps (a falling weight driving a generator) are a good solution for homes without electricity."
items.answer: They are a useful, safe low-cost option for basic lighting where there is no grid, though limited in power.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no fuel or batteries; safer than kerosene lamps; cheap to run. Arguments against: need re-lifting every 20–30 minutes; low light output. Supported judgement: They are a useful, safe low-cost option for basic lighting where there is no grid, though limited in power.

items.stem: In a Sankey diagram, what does a wider arrow show?
items.answer: More energy transferred
items.markingKey: More energy transferred. Width ∝ energy.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "An efficient machine wastes no energy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Even efficient machines waste some energy; efficiency is always less than 100%.
items.markingKey: Even efficient machines waste some energy; efficiency is always less than 100%. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the total energy output of a device equals its input.
items.answer: Energy is conserved; it is only transferred, so useful plus wasted energy equals the input. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Energy is conserved; it is only transferred, so useful plus wasted energy equals the input. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which Phasing out incandescent bulbs shows efficiency and policy.
items.answer: From 2009 the EU and many other countries phased out filament bulbs, which waste about 90–95% of their energy as heat, in favour of LEDs and compact fluorescent lamps. Lighting electricity use fell dramatically, reducing emissions and household bills.
items.markingKey: Context (From 2009 the EU and many other countries phased out filament bulbs, which waste about 90–95% of their energy as heat, in favour of LEDs and compact fluorescent lamps.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Lighting electricity use fell dramatically, reducing emissions and household bills. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to efficiency and policy.

items.stem: Chloé plans to investigate how the load lifted by an electric motor affects its efficiency. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: height lifted (1.0 m); voltage of the supply; the same motor and string; timing method
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: height lifted (1.0 m) – needed to calculate GPE; voltage of the supply – affects the input power; the same motor and string – different motors have different losses; timing method – affects energy calculation. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Freya measured the energy supplied to an electric kettle and the energy transferred to the water for different volumes of water.

Volume of water / cm³ | Efficiency / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
250 | 47 | 48 | 49
500 | 73 | 73 | 75
750 | 82 | 87 | 83
1000 | 90 | 88 | 85
1500 | 96 | 95 | 95

State the volume of water at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 750 cm³; range = 5 %; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 750 cm³; 1 range = max − min = 87 − 82 = 5 %; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Governments should ban inefficient appliances."
items.answer: Bans with clear labelling and support for low-income households have proven effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cuts energy use and emissions; saves money for households over time. Arguments against: efficient models may cost more to buy; limits consumer choice. Supported judgement: Bans with clear labelling and support for low-income households have proven effective.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the load lifted by an electric motor affects its efficiency. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): keep fingers away from the spinning axle; place a soft pad under the load. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. keep fingers away from the spinning axle; place a soft pad under the load); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A diagram with arrow widths proportional to the energy transferred"?
items.answer: Sankey diagram
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Sankey diagram.

items.stem: Distinguish between energy and power.
items.answer: Energy is the amount transferred, in J; power is how fast energy is transferred, in watts (J/s).
items.markingKey: Energy is the amount transferred, in J; power is how fast energy is transferred, in watts (J/s). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between power and energy.
items.answer: Energy is the amount transferred, in J; power is how fast energy is transferred, in watts (J/s).
items.markingKey: Energy is the amount transferred, in J; power is how fast energy is transferred, in watts (J/s). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A solar panel takes in 200 J of energy and transfers 36 J as electrical energy. Calculate its efficiency.
items.markingKey: M1 efficiency = useful ÷ total × 100 = 36 ÷ 200 × 100; A1 18%.

items.stem: A student claims: "Efficiency can be over 100% if the machine is very good." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: That would mean creating energy, which breaks the law of conservation of energy.
items.markingKey: That would mean creating energy, which breaks the law of conservation of energy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An electric kettle takes in 200 000 J and transfers 170 000 J to the water. Calculate its efficiency, describe where the wasted energy goes, draw (describe) a Sankey diagram, and suggest two improvements.
items.answer: Efficiency = 170 000 ÷ 200 000 × 100 = 85%. Wasted 30 000 J: heats the kettle body, air, and sound. Sankey: input arrow 200 kJ splitting into a wide 170 kJ useful arrow and a narrow 30 kJ wasted arrow. Improvements: better insulation (double wall), only boil the water needed, lid to reduce evaporation.
items.markingKey: Efficiency = 170 000 ÷ 200 000 × 100 = 85%. Wasted 30 000 J: heats the kettle body, air, and sound. Sankey: input arrow 200 kJ splitting into a wide 170 kJ useful arrow and a narrow 30 kJ wasted arrow. Improvements: better insulation (double wall), only boil the water needed, lid to reduce evaporation.

items.stem: Why are radiators often put under windows?
options: To set up a convection current that warms the whole room
items.answer: To set up a convection current that warms the whole room
items.markingKey: D. Warm air rises.

items.stem: A student claims: "Heat rises." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Hot fluids rise because they are less dense; thermal energy can be transferred in any direction by conduction and radiation.
items.markingKey: Hot fluids rise because they are less dense; thermal energy can be transferred in any direction by conduction and radiation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why loft insulation is made of fibreglass with lots of trapped air.
items.answer: Air is a poor conductor and trapping it in small pockets prevents convection currents.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Air is a poor conductor and trapping it in small pockets prevents convection currents. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Omar wrapped beakers of hot water in different numbers of layers of bubble wrap and measured the temperature drop in 15 minutes.

Layers of bubble wrap | Temperature drop / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 22.2 | 21.7 | 20.8
1 | 13.0 | 13.2 | 13.2
2 | 10.0 | 9.7 | 9.5
3 | 7.9 | 7.7 | 7.6
4 | 6.5 | 6.5 | 6.3

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The temperature drop decreases as the number of layers increases, with smaller improvements for each extra layer. Bubble wrap traps air, which is a poor conductor; more layers reduce conduction and convection, so the water loses energy more slowly.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The temperature drop decreases as the number of layers increases, with smaller improvements for each extra layer.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Bubble wrap traps air, which is a poor conductor; more layers reduce conduction and convection, so the water loses energy more slowly.

items.stem: Water in an uninsulated beaker cooled from 90 °C to 72 °C in 5 minutes. Calculate the average rate of cooling, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 3.6 °C/min; e.g. add a lid or wrap the beaker in insulation
items.markingKey: M1 (90 − 72) ÷ 5; A1 3.6 °C/min; B1 lid (reduces convection/evaporation) or insulation (traps air, reduces conduction).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Governments should pay for insulation in all older homes."
items.answer: Publicly funded insulation is a cost-effective climate measure, especially for low-income households, if done carefully.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cuts energy bills and carbon emissions; healthier warmer homes, fewer cold-related illnesses. Arguments against: high upfront public cost; some old buildings are hard to insulate without damage (damp). Supported judgement: Publicly funded insulation is a cost-effective climate measure, especially for low-income households, if done carefully.

items.stem: Define the term "convection current".
items.answer: The circulation of fluid caused by warm fluid rising and cool fluid sinking
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the circulation of fluid caused by warm fluid rising and cool fluid sinking. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a good reflector and a good emitter of radiation.
items.answer: A good emitter (matt black) radiates and absorbs infrared well; a good reflector (shiny silver) reflects infrared and emits and absorbs it poorly.
items.markingKey: A good emitter (matt black) radiates and absorbs infrared well; a good reflector (shiny silver) reflects infrared and emits and absorbs it poorly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between conduction and convection.
items.answer: Conduction transfers energy through vibrating particles in contact, mostly in solids; convection transfers energy by the bulk movement of a fluid as warm, less dense regions rise.
items.markingKey: Conduction transfers energy through vibrating particles in contact, mostly in solids; convection transfers energy by the bulk movement of a fluid as warm, less dense regions rise. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Sana is investigating how the colour of a can affects the rate at which hot water inside it cools. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: colour of the can surface (matt black, shiny silver, white, matt grey)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: colour of the can surface (matt black, shiny silver, white, matt grey) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Explain, using conduction, convection and radiation, how a house loses heat in winter, and evaluate three ways of reducing these losses.
items.answer: Conduction through walls, roof, windows and floors; convection of warm air out through gaps and in cavities; radiation from walls and roof. Reduce: loft insulation (traps air – cheap, quick payback); cavity wall insulation (stops convection in cavity – moderate cost); double glazing (air gap reduces conduction – expensive, long payback); draught excluders (cheap, reduce convection).
items.markingKey: Conduction through walls, roof, windows and floors; convection of warm air out through gaps and in cavities; radiation from walls and roof. Reduce: loft insulation (traps air – cheap, quick payback); cavity wall insulation (stops convection in cavity – moderate cost); double glazing (air gap reduces conduction – expensive, long payback); draught excluders (cheap, reduce convection).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "fossil fuel".
items.answer: Coal, oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of living things
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: coal, oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of living things. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between non-renewable resources and renewable resources.
items.answer: Renewable resources are naturally replaced and will not run out (wind, solar, hydro); non-renewable resources are finite and will run out (coal, oil, gas, uranium).
items.markingKey: Renewable resources are naturally replaced and will not run out (wind, solar, hydro); non-renewable resources are finite and will run out (coal, oil, gas, uranium). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why biofuels are sometimes described as carbon neutral.
items.answer: Plants absorb CO₂ while growing, roughly equal to the CO₂ released when the fuel burns. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Plants absorb CO₂ while growing, roughly equal to the CO₂ released when the fuel burns. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Elena writes: "Renewable energy resources cause no environmental problems." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Renewables have impacts too – hydroelectric dams flood valleys, wind farms affect landscapes and birds, biofuel crops use land.
items.markingKey: Renewables have impacts too – hydroelectric dams flood valleys, wind farms affect landscapes and birds, biofuel crops use land. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Iceland’s geothermal power, explain how it illustrates using local renewable resources.
items.answer: Iceland gets nearly all its electricity from hydroelectric and geothermal power and heats most homes with geothermal hot water. It shows a country’s geography can make renewables the main supply – but not every country has these resources.
items.markingKey: Context (Iceland gets nearly all its electricity from hydroelectric and geothermal power and heats most homes with geothermal hot water.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows a country’s geography can make renewables the main supply – but not every country has these resources. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to using local renewable resources.

items.stem: Tomás plans an investigation into how the angle of a solar panel to the light affects its output. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (angle between the panel and the light beam (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which renewable resource is the most reliable throughout the day and year?
items.answer: Geothermal
items.markingKey: B. Hot rocks are always hot.

items.stem: Distinguish between solar cells and solar water heaters.
items.answer: Solar cells transfer light energy into electricity; solar water heaters absorb infrared to heat water directly.
items.markingKey: Solar cells transfer light energy into electricity; solar water heaters absorb infrared to heat water directly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Arjun measured the power output of a model wind turbine at different fan speed settings.

Wind speed / m/s | Power output / mW: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
2 | 6 | 6 | 6
3 | 19 | 19 | 18
4 | 43 | 46 | 46
5 | 83 | 86 | 83
6 | 144 | 144 | 153

Calculate the mean power output when the wind speed was 3 m/s.
items.markingKey: M1 (19 + 19 + 18) ÷ 3; A1 18.7 mW (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the angle of a solar panel to the light affects its output, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: distance from the lamp (30 cm).
items.answer: light intensity falls with distance
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (distance from the lamp (30 cm)) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: light intensity falls with distance. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: "Every country should stop using fossil fuels within 10 years." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: A rapid but planned transition is needed; 10 years may be too fast for some countries without support.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: prevents dangerous climate change; improves air quality and health. Arguments against: renewable capacity and storage take time and money to build; poorer countries may need fossil fuels to develop; jobs depend on fossil-fuel industries. Supported judgement: A rapid but planned transition is needed; 10 years may be too fast for some countries without support. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "elastic potential energy".
items.answer: Energy stored in a stretched or squashed object
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: energy stored in a stretched or squashed object. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "efficiency"?
options: The fraction of input energy that is usefully transferred: useful output ÷ total input × 100%
Transfer of thermal energy by infrared waves, which can travel through a vacuum
Energy stored in a moving object
Transfer of thermal energy in liquids and gases by the movement of warmer, less dense fluid
items.answer: The fraction of input energy that is usefully transferred: useful output ÷ total input × 100%
items.markingKey: A. "efficiency" is the fraction of input energy that is usefully transferred: useful output ÷ total input × 100%.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Transfer of thermal energy through a material by vibrating particles passing energy to neighbours"?
items.answer: conduction
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of conduction.

items.stem: Briefly explain why fossil fuels are still widely used.
items.answer: They are reliable, energy-dense, and existing power stations, cars and infrastructure are built to use them.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are reliable, energy-dense, and existing power stations, cars and infrastructure are built to use them. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Sofia writes: "Only moving things have energy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Still objects can store energy in chemical, gravitational, elastic, thermal or nuclear stores.
items.markingKey: Still objects can store energy in chemical, gravitational, elastic, thermal or nuclear stores. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why wasted energy is hard to use.
items.answer: It is dissipated – spread thinly into the surroundings as thermal energy at a low temperature.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is dissipated – spread thinly into the surroundings as thermal energy at a low temperature. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how a vacuum flask keeps drinks hot.
items.answer: The vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvered walls reduce radiation; the stopper reduces convection and evaporation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvered walls reduce radiation; the stopper reduces convection and evaporation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Nuclear power is renewable because it produces no CO₂ when running." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Nuclear fuel (uranium) is finite, so it is non-renewable, even though it is low-carbon.
items.markingKey: Nuclear fuel (uranium) is finite, so it is non-renewable, even though it is low-carbon. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between an energy pathway and an energy store.
items.answer: An energy store is where energy is held (kinetic, chemical, thermal …); a pathway is how energy moves between stores (by forces, heating, electricity, radiation).
items.markingKey: An energy store is where energy is held (kinetic, chemical, thermal …); a pathway is how energy moves between stores (by forces, heating, electricity, radiation). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Kenji measured the energy supplied to an electric kettle and the energy transferred to the water for different volumes of water.

Volume of water / cm³ | Efficiency / %: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
250 | 44 | 44 | 42
500 | 68 | 68 | 68
750 | 78 | 76 | 78
1000 | 83 | 78 | 80
1500 | 83 | 84 | 87

Calculate the mean efficiency when the volume of water was 1000 cm³.
items.markingKey: M1 (83 + 78 + 80) ÷ 3; A1 80.3 % (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Briefly describe Passive house design and explain what it reveals about reducing thermal energy transfer.
items.answer: Passive houses use thick insulation, triple glazing, airtight construction and heat-recovery ventilation, needing up to 90% less heating energy than typical homes. Shows how controlling conduction, convection and radiation cuts energy use and emissions.
items.markingKey: Context (Passive houses use thick insulation, triple glazing, airtight construction and heat-recovery ventilation, needing up to 90% less heating energy than typical homes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Shows how controlling conduction, convection and radiation cuts energy use and emissions. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to reducing thermal energy transfer.

items.stem: A town needs an average power of 20 MW. Each wind turbine has a maximum output of 2 MW but on average produces only 40% of this. How many turbines are needed? Explain why the average is less than the maximum.
items.answer: 25 turbines; the wind does not always blow at the ideal speed
items.markingKey: M1 average per turbine = 2 × 40/100 = 0.8 MW; M1 20 ÷ 0.8 = 25; A1 round up to 25; B1 wind speed varies.

items.stem: A ball is dropped from 45 m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before it hits the ground (g = 10 N/kg).
items.answer: 30 m/s
items.markingKey: M1 GPE lost = KE gained: mgh = ½mv²; M1 v = √(2 × 10 × 45); A1 30 m/s.

items.stem: A filament bulb is 20% efficient and is supplied with 800 J. Calculate the energy wasted and state where most of it goes.
items.answer: 640 J; mostly dissipated as thermal energy in the surroundings
items.markingKey: M1 useful = 160 J; M1 wasted = 800 − 160; A1 640 J; B1 thermal store of surroundings.

items.stem:
Freya wrapped beakers of hot water in different numbers of layers of bubble wrap and measured the temperature drop in 15 minutes.

Layers of bubble wrap | Temperature drop / °C: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 21.5 | 21.8 | 21.2
1 | 13.0 | 13.2 | 13.4
2 | 10.0 | 9.9 | 9.4
3 | 7.8 | 5.1 | 7.6
4 | 6.0 | 6.0 | 6.2

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean temperature drop at 3, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 5.1 °C (trial 2 at 3); mean = 7.70 °C
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (5.1) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 7.70 °C.

items.stem: A town needs an average power of 50 MW. Each wind turbine has a maximum output of 4 MW but on average produces only 40% of this. How many turbines are needed? Explain why the average is less than the maximum.
items.answer: 32 turbines; the wind does not always blow at the ideal speed
items.markingKey: M1 average per turbine = 4 × 40/100 = 1.6 MW; M1 50 ÷ 1.6 = 31.2; A1 round up to 32; B1 wind speed varies.

items.stem: Write a risk assessment for an investigation into how the drop height of a ball affects its bounce height. Identify two hazards, the risk each poses and how each risk will be reduced, and explain one ethical or environmental consideration.
items.answer: Key hazard(s): keep the area clear; do not stand on chairs – use a stable step. For each hazard: state what could go wrong, how likely/serious it is, and the precaution. Ethical/environmental: e.g. minimise waste and dispose of chemicals correctly, treat living organisms and volunteers with respect and consent.
items.markingKey: 2 two relevant hazards with the risk explained (e.g. keep the area clear; do not stand on chairs – use a stable step); 2 a specific precaution for each; 1 relevant ethical or environmental consideration.

items.stem: "Governments should ban inefficient appliances." Discuss.
items.answer: Bans with clear labelling and support for low-income households have proven effective.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cuts energy use and emissions; saves money for households over time. Arguments against: efficient models may cost more to buy; limits consumer choice. Supported judgement: Bans with clear labelling and support for low-income households have proven effective. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Aiko plans an investigation into how the colour of a can affects the rate at which hot water inside it cools. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (colour of the can surface (matt black, shiny silver, white, matt grey)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: A small island community currently uses diesel generators for electricity. Evaluate replacing them with a mix of wind turbines and solar panels.
items.answer: Benefits: no fuel costs or imports, no CO₂ or air pollution, renewable. Problems: output varies with weather and time – needs battery storage or keeping a diesel backup; high initial cost; visual impact; maintenance skills needed. Conclusion: a mix of wind and solar (complementary – windy winters, sunny summers) with batteries could supply most needs, with diesel as backup.
items.markingKey: Benefits: no fuel costs or imports, no CO₂ or air pollution, renewable. Problems: output varies with weather and time – needs battery storage or keeping a diesel backup; high initial cost; visual impact; maintenance skills needed. Conclusion: a mix of wind and solar (complementary – windy winters, sunny summers) with batteries could supply most needs, with diesel as backup.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "kinetic energy"?
options: Energy stored in an object because of its height above the ground
Energy stored in a moving object
A diagram with arrow widths proportional to the energy transferred
Coal, oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of living things
items.answer: Energy stored in a moving object
items.markingKey: B. "kinetic energy" is energy stored in a moving object.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "useful energy".
items.answer: Energy transferred to the store we want
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: energy transferred to the store we want. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "insulator"?
options: Energy stored in a stretched or squashed object
A material that is a poor conductor of thermal energy
Transfer of thermal energy in liquids and gases by the movement of warmer, less dense fluid
Energy transferred to stores that are not wanted, usually thermal energy of the surroundings
items.answer: A material that is a poor conductor of thermal energy
items.markingKey: B. "insulator" is a material that is a poor conductor of thermal energy.

items.stem: Explain the difference between non-renewable resources and renewable resources.
items.answer: Renewable resources are naturally replaced and will not run out (wind, solar, hydro); non-renewable resources are finite and will run out (coal, oil, gas, uranium).
items.markingKey: Renewable resources are naturally replaced and will not run out (wind, solar, hydro); non-renewable resources are finite and will run out (coal, oil, gas, uranium). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Only moving things have energy." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Still objects can store energy in chemical, gravitational, elastic, thermal or nuclear stores.
items.markingKey: Still objects can store energy in chemical, gravitational, elastic, thermal or nuclear stores. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Efficiency can be over 100% if the machine is very good." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: That would mean creating energy, which breaks the law of conservation of energy.
items.markingKey: That would mean creating energy, which breaks the law of conservation of energy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Priya writes: "Heat rises." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Hot fluids rise because they are less dense; thermal energy can be transferred in any direction by conduction and radiation.
items.markingKey: Hot fluids rise because they are less dense; thermal energy can be transferred in any direction by conduction and radiation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why wind turbines alone cannot supply all of a country’s electricity.
items.answer: Wind speed varies, so output is unreliable; storage or backup from other sources is needed when the wind is low.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Wind speed varies, so output is unreliable; storage or backup from other sources is needed when the wind is low. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an energy store and an energy pathway.
items.answer: An energy store is where energy is held (kinetic, chemical, thermal …); a pathway is how energy moves between stores (by forces, heating, electricity, radiation).
items.markingKey: An energy store is where energy is held (kinetic, chemical, thermal …); a pathway is how energy moves between stores (by forces, heating, electricity, radiation). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mateo is investigating how the load lifted by an electric motor affects its efficiency. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: mass lifted (100, 200, 300, 400, 500 g) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Water in an uninsulated beaker cooled from 80 °C to 56 °C in 15 minutes. Calculate the average rate of cooling, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 1.6 °C/min; e.g. add a lid or wrap the beaker in insulation
items.markingKey: M1 (80 − 56) ÷ 15; A1 1.6 °C/min; B1 lid (reduces convection/evaporation) or insulation (traps air, reduces conduction).

items.stem: Diego is investigating how the angle of a solar panel to the light affects its output. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: angle between the panel and the light beam (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: angle between the panel and the light beam (0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 60 kg object moving at 20 m/s (KE = ½mv²).
A solar panel is 18% efficient and is supplied with 800 J. Calculate the energy wasted and state where most of it goes.
items.answer: 656 J; mostly dissipated as thermal energy in the surroundings
items.markingKey: M1 useful = 144 J; M1 wasted = 800 − 144; A1 656 J; B1 thermal store of surroundings.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Iceland’s geothermal power shows using local renewable resources.
items.answer: Iceland gets nearly all its electricity from hydroelectric and geothermal power and heats most homes with geothermal hot water. It shows a country’s geography can make renewables the main supply – but not every country has these resources.
items.markingKey: Context (Iceland gets nearly all its electricity from hydroelectric and geothermal power and heats most homes with geothermal hot water.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It shows a country’s geography can make renewables the main supply – but not every country has these resources. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to using local renewable resources.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Gravity-powered lamps (a falling weight driving a generator) are a good solution for homes without electricity."
items.answer: They are a useful, safe low-cost option for basic lighting where there is no grid, though limited in power.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no fuel or batteries; safer than kerosene lamps; cheap to run. Arguments against: need re-lifting every 20–30 minutes; low light output. Supported judgement: They are a useful, safe low-cost option for basic lighting where there is no grid, though limited in power.

items.stem: Mateo plans an investigation into how the load lifted by an electric motor affects its efficiency. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (mass lifted (100, 200, 300, 400, 500 g)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.

items.stem: "Governments should pay for insulation in all older homes." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Publicly funded insulation is a cost-effective climate measure, especially for low-income households, if done carefully.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cuts energy bills and carbon emissions; healthier warmer homes, fewer cold-related illnesses. Arguments against: high upfront public cost; some old buildings are hard to insulate without damage (damp). Supported judgement: Publicly funded insulation is a cost-effective climate measure, especially for low-income households, if done carefully. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: "Hydroelectric dams are the best renewable resource." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Hydroelectricity is excellent where suitable, but local social and environmental costs must be weighed.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: reliable and can respond quickly to demand; can store energy (pumped storage). Arguments against: flood valleys, destroying habitats and displacing people; only possible in suitable mountainous places. Supported judgement: Hydroelectricity is excellent where suitable, but local social and environmental costs must be weighed. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.
